title: What an LLM learns: guessing a hidden word

blocks.main: **An LLM (large language model) learns by guessing a hidden word and then changing its weights a little.** In the sentence "The chef cracks the," the last word is hidden. The model reads the four words before the gap. Then it has to predict the word that fills the gap.
sub: Each word before the gap gives a clue about the hidden word. These clue relationships are called **interdependencies** (one part of a sequence helps predict another part).
The model does not know the answer, so it spreads its bets. A bet is the probability the model gives to one word. It bets the most on "egg," less on "nut" and the least on "code."

**Learning means nudging the weights (changing each weight a little) so that these guesses get better.** After the true word is revealed, the weights change a little. Because of that change, the right word gets a bigger bet next time.
blocks.end: The same idea holds when the signal (the sequence the model reads) contains words, sounds and images. The model still guesses a hidden piece and nudges its weights, so the way it learns stays the same.

title: Turning speech and images into rows of vectors

blocks.main: **An LLM can only read a row of vectors (lists of numbers), so speech and images have to be converted first.** Text, speech and images arrive in three different forms.
sub: **Text** is already a row of pieces, such as "Now," "crack," "the" and "egg," and each piece can become one vector.
**Speech** is air pressure changing in time, and there are no words in the sound itself.
An **image** is a grid of light, and it contains no words either.
blocks.end: So the first job is a conversion. Speech and images both have to become rows of vectors, because that is all the LLM can read.

blocks.main: **Speech is turned into a row of vectors by slicing it in time.** The sound is cut into short slices, and each slice is called a **frame**. Each slice is about 20 milliseconds long.
sub: The slices go through a **speech encoder** (a neural network that was trained on a large amount of audio). One vector comes out for each slice.
**One second of speech becomes 50 vectors.** This is because each slice is about 20 milliseconds long, and 50 slices of that length fill one second. Each slice gives one vector.
The vectors stay in time order. The first slice gives the first vector, and the last slice gives the last vector.
blocks.end: So speech is now a row, just like a sentence, and the LLM can read it one vector after another.

blocks.main: **An image is turned into a row of vectors by cutting it into patches.** A **patch** is one small square of the image. A grid cuts the image of an egg in a pan into 16 patches.
sub: The patches are laid out in a row in **reading order** (left to right along the top, then left to right along the next line down). This turns the image into a sequence, like a sentence.
The patches go through a **vision encoder**. One vector comes out for each patch, so 16 patches give 16 vectors.
Real systems use much smaller patches of 14 to 16 pixels. Smaller patches mean more patches for the same image, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.
blocks.end: So both conversions follow the same steps. The signal is cut into small pieces, the pieces are kept in order, and an encoder gives one vector for each piece.

title: One row, three senses: cross-modal dependencies

blocks.main: **Image patches, speech frames and words can all be placed in one row, and the model guesses the hidden piece.** The image patches come first, the speech frames come next, and the words come last. The words are "Now," "crack" and "the," and the word after them is hidden.
sub: The words before the gap still give clues, the same as in a row that holds only text.
Clues now also come from the other senses. A patch that contains an egg helps the model guess the hidden word. The sound of cracking helps too.
A link between two different kinds of signal is called a **cross-modal dependency**.
blocks.end: So the game is exactly the same as before. The only new thing is that some of the clues come from other senses.

blocks.main: **"Three cute puppies" is one event given in three forms, and training puts all three in one row.** The first form is an image of three puppies, cut into 18 patches. The second form is the phrase spoken aloud. The third form is the three written words.
sub: The spoken phrase is shown as a **spectrogram** (a display of a sound laid out in time). Time runs from left to right. Higher up means a higher frequency. A darker area means more energy.
Each thin column of the spectrogram is one frame. Each word has its own stretch of time, with "three" first and "puppies" last.
The voice is a speech synthesizer (an MBROLA diphone voice). It is not a recording of a person.
blocks.end: So the image, the sound and the words are three views of one event. In training, one piece of the row is hidden, and the model has to guess it.

title: The three training examples: hidden word, hidden sound frame, hidden image patch

blocks.main: **In training example 1, the hidden piece is a word, and the image and the sound settle the guess.** The row holds the image, then the sound, then the words "three" and "cute." The word after "cute" is hidden.
sub: With the words alone, the bets are spread out. This is because many endings fit after "three cute," such as "kittens," "puppies" and "babies."
With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on "puppies." This is because the image contains puppies, and the sound contains the spoken word "puppies."
The true word is then revealed, and the model is graded on how much it bet on that word. The model bet 0.85 on "puppies."
blocks.end: So the nudge to the weights is small. This is because the model bet a lot on the true word, so the error is small, and a small error moves the weights only a little.

blocks.main: **In training example 2, the hidden piece is a frame of sound, and three clues help the model guess it.** The row is put in a new order, with the image first, then the words, then the sound. This is like teaching the model to speak a sentence it was given. The sound is predicted frame by frame, from left to right.
sub: The frames already heard are the first clue. The voice and the **formants** (frequency regions with strong energy) change smoothly, so the last few frames say a lot about the next one.
The words are the second clue. They say which sound should come next, and here it is the vowel in "pup."
The image is the third clue. It contains puppies, so it backs up the words. It is a weaker clue here.
A frame is a column of numbers. Each number is how much energy there is in one frequency band. The guess is close to the true frame, but it is not exact.
blocks.end: So the error is how far each guessed number is from the true number, and that error nudges the weights.

blocks.main: **In training example 3, the hidden piece is a patch of the image, and the biggest error is the colour.** The row is put in a new order again, with the words first, then the sound, then the image. This is like teaching the model to draw what it was told. The patches are predicted in reading order.
sub: The patches already drawn are the first clue. Above the hidden patch is background. To its left are two puppies, so the model has seen what a puppy in this image looks like.
The words are the second clue. "Three" says a third puppy must appear, because only two are drawn. "Puppies" says to expect dog ears.
The sound is the third clue. It carries the same words, so it backs up the text.
The model guesses a blurry puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies. The true puppy is dark.
blocks.end: So the biggest error is the colour. This is because no clue in the words, the sound or the patches already drawn said the third puppy would be dark. Only systems that also produce images are trained this way.

title: Every piece can be the hidden one: two kinds of clue

blocks.main: **Any piece of the row can be the hidden one, and each sense gives a clue for it.** The hidden piece can be a word, a sound frame or an image patch.
sub: For a **hidden word**, the words "three cute" call for a plural noun, the sound has just spoken the word, and the image contains puppies.
For a **hidden frame**, the words say which sound comes next, the voice and the formants carry on, and the image backs up which word is being said.
For a **hidden patch**, the word "three" says one more puppy is coming, the sound gives the same words in heard form, and the fur and the background carry on.
blocks.end: So a clue from the same sense says how the signal continues, and clues from the other senses say what the thing is. Training on all three senses together helps, because each sense fills gaps that the others leave.

title: Talking back, what is new and what stays the same

blocks.main: **The model speaks by predicting codes for sound, and a decoder turns the codes back into sound.** First, sound is compressed into discrete codes (separate numbered units), such as 417, 82 and 903. Each code works like a new word added to the vocabulary.
sub: The model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word. So speaking is the same guessing game again.
A **decoder** then turns the row of predicted codes back into a sound wave that can be heard.
blocks.end: So the model gives the codes, and the decoder gives the sound.

blocks.main: **Three things are new when a model is trained on words, sounds and images, and one thing stays the same.** The first new thing is a **shared currency**, in which everything becomes vectors in one row. The second is **data where the senses appear together**. The third is **a schedule that protects what was already learned**.
sub: What stays the same is the learning rule, which is to find the dependencies in the signal.
blocks.end: So the model still guesses a hidden piece and nudges its weights. The signal has only become wider, because it now holds words, sounds and images.
